title: Conclusion
paragraphs: I have now nearly reached the end of my inquiry. Up to this point, in speaking of the future destiny of the United States, I have tried to divide my subject into distinct sections, so that I could study each one with more attention. My present aim is to take in the whole from a single vantage point. The observations I shall make will be less detailed, but they will be more certain. I shall see each object less distinctly, but I shall identify the main facts more surely. A traveler who has just left the walls of an immense city climbs the neighboring hill. As he moves farther off, he loses sight of the people he has just left; their houses are confused in a dense mass. He can no longer make out the public squares, and he can barely trace the major thoroughfares. But his eye has less difficulty following the boundaries of the city, and for the first time he sees the shape of the vast whole. Such is the future destiny of the British race in North America as I see it. The details of the enormous picture are shrouded in shadow, but I form a clear idea of the entire subject.

The territory now occupied or possessed by the United States of America makes up about one-twentieth of the habitable earth. But extensive as these boundaries are, one should not assume that the Anglo-American race will always remain within them. In fact, it has already pushed far beyond them.

There was once a time when we too might have created a great French nation in the American wilds, to balance the influence of the English over the destinies of the New World. France once held a territory in North America scarcely smaller than the whole of Europe. The three greatest rivers of that continent then flowed through her dominions. The Indian tribes that lived between the mouth of the St. Lawrence and the delta of the Mississippi knew no language but ours, and all the European settlements scattered across that immense region recalled the traditions of our country. Louisbourg, Montmorency, Duquesne, St. Louis, Vincennes, New Orleans — such were the names they bore — are words dear to France and familiar to our ears.

But a combination of circumstances, which it would be tedious to list, *m has deprived us of this magnificent inheritance. Wherever the French settlers were few in number and only partly established, they have disappeared. Those who remain are gathered in a small stretch of country and are now subject to other laws. The 400,000 French inhabitants of Lower Canada are, at present, the remnant of an old nation lost in the midst of a new people. A foreign population is growing around them without pause and on every side. It is already spreading among the country's ancient masters, dominating their cities and corrupting their language. This population is identical to that of the United States. So it is accurate to say that the British race is not confined within the borders of the Union, since it already extends to the northeast.

m [ The first of these circumstances is that nations accustomed to free institutions and local government are better able than any others to found prosperous colonies. The habit of thinking and governing for oneself is essential in a new country, where success necessarily depends, to a great extent, on the individual effort of the settlers.]

To the northwest there is nothing but a few insignificant Russian settlements. But to the southwest, Mexico presents a barrier to the Anglo-Americans. So, strictly speaking, the Spaniards and the Anglo-Americans are the only two races that divide the New World between them. The boundary separating them has been fixed by treaty. But although the terms of that treaty are extremely favorable to the Anglo-Americans, I have no doubt that they will soon breach this arrangement. Vast provinces extending beyond the frontiers of the Union toward Mexico are still uninhabited. The natives of the United States will get there before the rightful occupants of these empty regions. They will take possession of the soil and establish social institutions, so that when the legal owner finally arrives, he will find the wilderness under cultivation and strangers quietly settled in the midst of his inheritance. *n
n [ [This was soon accomplished, and before long both Texas and California became part of the United States. The Russian settlements were acquired by purchase.]]

The lands of the New World belong to the first occupant, and they are the natural reward of the swiftest pioneer. Even the countries that are already populated will have some difficulty in protecting themselves from this invasion. I have already referred to what is happening in the province of Texas. The inhabitants of the United States keep migrating to Texas, where they buy land. And though they conform to the laws of the country, they are gradually founding the empire of their own language and their own customs. The province of Texas is still part of the Mexican dominions, but it will soon contain no Mexicans. The same thing has happened whenever the Anglo-Americans have come into contact with populations of a different origin.

There is no denying that the British race has gained an astonishing preponderance over all the other European races in the New World, and that it is far superior to them in civilization, in industry, and in power. As long as it is surrounded only by desert or thinly populated countries, as long as it meets no dense populations on its route through which it cannot force its way, it will certainly keep spreading. The lines drawn by treaties will not stop it; it will cross these imaginary barriers wherever they stand.

The geographical position of the British race in the New World is especially favorable to its rapid increase. Above its northern frontiers stretch the icy regions of the Pole, and a few degrees below its southern boundaries lies the burning climate of the Equator. The Anglo-Americans are therefore placed in the most temperate and habitable zone of the continent.

It is commonly supposed that the astonishing growth of population in the United States came after their Declaration of Independence. But this is a mistake: the population grew as rapidly under the colonial system as it does today — that is, it doubled in about twenty-two years. But this ratio, which is now applied to millions, was then applied to thousands of inhabitants. And the same fact that was barely noticeable a century ago is now obvious to every observer.

The British subjects in Canada, who are dependent on a king, multiply and spread almost as rapidly as the British settlers of the United States, who live under a republican government. During the War of Independence, which lasted eight years, the population kept growing at the same rate without interruption. Although powerful Indian nations allied with the English then existed on the western frontiers, westward emigration was never checked. While the enemy laid waste the shores of the Atlantic, Kentucky, the western parts of Pennsylvania, and the States of Vermont and Maine were filling with inhabitants. Nor did the unsettled state of the Constitution that followed the war prevent the population from growing or stop its advance across the wilderness. So the difference of laws, the varying conditions of peace and war, of order and of anarchy, have had no perceptible effect on the gradual development of the Anglo-Americans. This is easy to understand. For the fact is that no causes are general enough to exert a simultaneous influence over the whole of so vast a territory. One part of the country always offers a sure refuge from the calamities afflicting another part; and however great the evil may be, the remedy at hand is greater still.

One should not, then, imagine that the momentum of the British race in the New World can be halted. The breakup of the Union, the hostilities that might follow, the abolition of republican institutions, and the tyrannical government that might succeed them, may slow this momentum, but they cannot prevent it from ultimately fulfilling the destinies reserved for that race. No power on earth can close off to the emigrants that fertile wilderness which offers resources to every industry and a refuge from every want. Future events, whatever their nature, will not deprive the Americans of their climate or of their inland seas, of their great rivers or of their rich soil. Nor will bad laws, revolutions, and anarchy be able to erase that love of prosperity and that spirit of enterprise which seem to be the distinctive characteristics of their race, or to extinguish the knowledge that guides them on their way.

Thus, amid the uncertain future, one event at least is certain. At a time that may be called near — for we are speaking of the life of a nation — the Anglo-Americans alone will cover the immense space contained between the polar regions and the tropics, stretching from the coasts of the Atlantic to the shores of the Pacific Ocean. The territory likely to be occupied at some future time by the Anglo-Americans may be estimated as equal to three-quarters of Europe in extent. *o The climate of the Union is on the whole preferable to that of Europe, and its natural advantages are no less great. It is therefore clear that its population will in time match our own. Europe, divided as it is among so many different nations, and torn as it has been by incessant wars and the barbarous manners of the Middle Ages, has nevertheless reached a population of 410 inhabitants per square league. *p What is there to prevent the United States from having as dense a population in time?

o [ The United States already extend over a territory equal to half of Europe. The area of Europe is 500,000 square leagues, and its population 205,000,000 inhabitants. ("Malte Brun," bk. 114, vol. vi, p. 4.)

[This calculation is given in French leagues, which were in use when the author wrote. Twenty years later, in 1850, the area of the United States had been extended to 3,306,865 square miles of territory, which is about the area of Europe.]]
p [ See "Malte Brun," bk. 116, vol. vi, p. 92.]

Many ages must pass before the various offshoots of the British race in America cease to display the same homogeneous characteristics. And the time cannot be foreseen when a permanent inequality of conditions will be established in the New World. Whatever differences may arise — from peace or war, from freedom or oppression, from prosperity or want — between the destinies of the various descendants of the great Anglo-American family, they will at least preserve an analogous social condition, and they will hold in common the customs and opinions to which that social condition has given rise.

In the Middle Ages, the tie of religion was strong enough to imbue all the different populations of Europe with the same civilization. The British of the New World have a thousand other reciprocal ties, and they live at a time when the tendency to equality is general among mankind. The Middle Ages were a period when everything was broken up, when each people, each province, each city, and each family had a strong tendency to maintain its distinct individuality. At the present time an opposite tendency seems to prevail, and the nations seem to be moving toward unity. Our means of intellectual exchange unite the most remote parts of the earth, and it is impossible for people to remain strangers to each other, or to be ignorant of the events taking place in any corner of the globe. The result is that there is less difference today between the Europeans and their descendants in the New World than there was between certain towns in the thirteenth century separated only by a river. If this tendency toward assimilation brings foreign nations closer together, it must all the more prevent the descendants of the same people from becoming strangers to each other.

The time will therefore come when one hundred and fifty million people will be living in North America, *q equal in condition, the offspring of one race, owing their origin to the same cause, and preserving the same civilization, the same language, the same religion, the same habits, the same manners, shaped by the same opinions propagated under the same forms. The rest is uncertain, but this is certain. And it is a fact new to the world — a fact loaded with such momentous consequences that it defies even the efforts of the imagination.
q [ This would be a population proportionate to that of Europe, figured at an average rate of 410 inhabitants per square league.]

There are at this moment two great nations in the world which seem to be moving toward the same end, although they started from different points: I mean the Russians and the Americans. Both of them have grown up unnoticed, and while the attention of mankind was turned elsewhere, they have suddenly assumed a most prominent place among the nations. The world learned of their existence and their greatness at nearly the same time.

All other nations seem to have nearly reached their natural limits and to be charged only with maintaining their power. But these two are still in the act of growth. *r All the others are stopped, or continue to advance with great difficulty; these are proceeding with ease and with speed along a path to which the human eye can assign no end. The American struggles against the natural obstacles that oppose him; the Russian's adversaries are men. The one combats the wilderness and savage life; the other combats civilization with all its weapons and its arts. The conquests of the one are therefore won by the plowshare; those of the other by the sword. The Anglo-American relies on personal interest to accomplish his ends, and gives free rein to the unguided efforts and common sense of the citizens. The Russian concentrates all the authority of society in a single arm. The main instrument of the one is freedom; of the other, servitude. Their starting points are different, and their paths are not the same. Yet each of them seems marked out by the will of Heaven to sway the destinies of half the globe.
r [ Russia is the country in the Old World where population increases most rapidly in proportion.]
